title: Seventy sent (Luke 10:1–20)
hookLine: sent in pairs: say peace to this house first

lines: WHAT DO YOU SAY AT THE DOOR?
cards: What's the first thing you say when you walk into someone's home? Hi. Sorry I'm late.
Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem now, and he sends out a much bigger group than the twelve.
In the King James words: "the Lord appointed other seventy also, and sent them two and two before his face into every city and place, whither he himself would come." Two by two, so no one goes alone.
Ahead of him, preparing the way. And first, he tells them exactly what to say at the door.

teach.b: First, the honest warning: "The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few." And: "behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves." Not soldiers.
Lambs. The packing list is lighter than ever: no purse, no bag, no shoes, and no stopping to chat with everyone on the road.

teach.h: FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: Then the doorway: "And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house."
Behind the Greek word for peace stands the Hebrew greeting shalom, which reaches past the absence of fighting toward wholeness and well-being.
Then a beautiful detail: "And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again."

teach.h: IF REFUSED, IT RETURNS TO YOU.
teach.b: Peace is like something you set down in a room. If someone there is open to it, it stays. If not, it comes back to you; you don't lose it by offering it.
Stay in one house, he says. Eat what they put in front of you. Heal the sick.
Say the kingdom of God has come near. And if a town won't welcome you, shake off the dust and move on. The seventy come back overjoyed: even the demons obey us in your name!
Jesus gently turns their joy: "rejoice, because your names are written in heaven."

teach.h: FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.
teach.b: Not in the power they had, but in being known by name. Luke never names them; they aren't the twelve.

how: In the Book of Common Prayer, the order for the visitation of the sick opens with "Peace be to this house," and some Christians use the same words when blessing a home.

games.q: you're one of the seventy, at the door of a stranger's house. what do you say first?
games.why: peace comes first. if a son of peace is there, it rests on the house; if not, it returns to you.

practice: Bring to mind a home you'll walk into soon: your own after work, a friend's, a parent's, maybe one where things are tense or simply tired.
Picture yourself at the door bringing peace in before a word about traffic or dinner, like setting down a gift, and then letting go of whether it's received.
If you pray, say the line from Luke silently at the door; if you don't, simply bring calm in with you.

wordCard.voice: Seventy sent. Jesus sends out seventy, two by two, as lambs among wolves, and tells them to say first, at every door: peace be to this house.

orig.note: Greek: peace. in Jesus' world the greeting was shalom: wholeness and well-being.

carryVoice: Your line: peace be to this house. It was a week of a hidden woman and a waking girl, five loaves, a daily cross, a shining face, a child, a road, and seventy at the door. Another week on the path.
